extracted.intended_audience: employers, lawyers, policymakers, and public commenters on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting comments or complying with the FTC's rulemaking and final rule on non-compete clauses, including notice requirements, definitions (NDA/trade secret), scope (who is covered), and related evidentiary and legal standards cited by the Commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly compensated employee threshold (85th percentile)
rubrics_metrics.description: This threshold is based on the 85th percentile of earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Part IV.C.4.b.; DOL proposed a threshold at $143,998 (the 85th percentile at the time of the 2023 FLSA NPRM). Historical context: original 2004 HCE test at $100,000 exceeded earnings of 93.7% of salaried workers. (Cites: 2023 FLSA NPRM, BLS research series.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice required only for existing non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final rule, notice is only required for existing non-competes, i.e., those that have not elapsed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required notice is characterized as a routine disclosure of valuable, factual information that does not implicate the First Amendment (citing Milavetz, Gallop & Milavetz v. United States and Zauderer). The Commission adopts the notice requirement to ensure workers do not wrongly believe they remain bound and to address the in terrorem effect of non-competes, based on Commission expertise and empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice delivery method—use of last known address or email
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice language mirrors other federal regulations requiring notice by mail to the person's last known address or last known email address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM language mirrors provisions such as 17 CFR 9.11, 29 CFR 38.79, and 16 CFR 318.5 which provide for written notification at an individual's last known address or email (or another known method of contacting the complainant in writing). See §910.2(b) and related citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice content and employer recordkeeping for contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may be required to use retained contact information (addresses, emails, telephone numbers) to provide notice as described in §910.2(b)(2)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers already have many record-keeping requirements under federal and state laws (e.g., IRS Pub. 15 requires keeping employment tax records for at least 4 years; USCIS Handbook M-274 requires retaining Form I-9 which includes addresses and contact info). See related citations on recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/accessibility considerations for notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission recognizes linguistic diversity (e.g., nearly 68 million people spoke a language other than English at home in 2019) and references proposed §910.3 concerning language/accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Census Bureau language statistics and NPRM proposed §910.3 and related discussion (NPRM at 3514-15). Consideration of language needs is part of designing notice requirements to reach non-English speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's definition/use of 'NDA'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission uses the term 'NDA' to refer to contractual provisions designed to protect trade secrets or other business information that has economic value; NDAs may also be used to protect information about discrimination, harassment, sexual assault, corporate wrongdoing, or disparaging information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes that NDAs used to protect non-employment-related matters have been widely criticized for harmful effects on workers. See Rachel S. Arnow-Richman et al., and other cited scholarship criticizing certain NDA uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret definition (UTSA/DTSA/EEA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the UTSA, a 'trade secret' is information that (1) derives independent economic value from not being generally known and (2) is the subject of reasonable efforts to maintain its secrecy; DTSA and EEA use a similar definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites UTSA sec. 1(4), 18 U.S.C. 1839(3), and Supreme Court authority requiring 'some novelty' for a trade secret (Kewanee Oil Co. v. Bicron Corp.). Examples: customer lists, methods of production, secret formulas can be trade secrets if secrecy and economic value requirements met. See case law such as Confold Pac., Inc. v. Polaris Indus., Inc., and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement for trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has held that 'some novelty' is required for information to be a trade secret, because 'that which does not possess novelty is usually known.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Kewanee Oil Co. v. Bicron Corp.; courts recognize not all customer lists or business information are trade secrets—depends on facts and secrecy efforts. See U.S. West Commc'ns v. Off. of Consumer Advoc., Guy Carpenter v. Provenzale, and other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitable disclosure doctrine—limited and controversial
rubrics_metrics.description: In some States, courts may enjoin a worker from working for a competitor where it is 'inevitable' the worker will disclose trade secrets in performing duties; the doctrine is controversial and not universally adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PepsiCo, Inc. v. Redmond applied inevitable disclosure; other states have declined adoption (Bayer Corp. v. Roche Molecular Sys.) or required high evidentiary burdens (LeJeune v. Coin Acceptors). See discussion of controversy and evidentiary standards; see Godfrey, Inevitable Disclosure of Trade Secrets for broader analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common enterprise factors for disregarding corporate separateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider a variety of factors to find a 'common enterprise' and disregard corporate separateness, including (1) maintaining officers and employees in common, (2) operating under common control, (3) sharing offices, (4) commingling funds, and (5) sharing advertising and marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one factor is controlling; courts consider the pattern and framework of the whole enterprise (quoting FTC v. Wash. Data Res. and Del. Watch Co. v. FTC). See related cases (FTC v. E.M.A. Nationwide, FTC v. WV Universal Mgmt., LLC) about joint-and-several liability and common enterprise findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint and several liability where a common enterprise exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have imposed joint and several liability when a common enterprise exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites FTC v. WV Universal Mgmt., LLC (11th Cir. 2017) and other authority demonstrating when corporate form may be disregarded for liability purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addyston Pipe test for partial restraints of trade (sale of business)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants in partial restraint of trade are generally upheld as valid when they are agreements by the seller of a business not to compete with the buyer, but before such agreements are upheld the court must find the restraints are 'reasonably necessary' to the enjoyment by the buyer of the property, goodwill, or interest bought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites United States v. Addyston Pipe & Steel Co. and later cases (Polk Bros. v. Forest City Enters.) applying the 'reasonably necessary' test in the sale-of-business context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust and Section 5 — Commission will not accept justifications where courts have not
rubrics_metrics.description: For provisions of the antitrust laws where courts have not accepted justifications as part of the legal analysis, the Commission will similarly not accept justifications when such claims are pursued through section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Atlantic Refining Co., FTC v. Texaco, L.G. Balfour Co. v. FTC, and others; also cites cases where courts rejected procompetitive justifications in contexts like group boycotts (Ind. Fed'n of Dentists) and other antitrust precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'bona fide'
rubrics_metrics.description: Black's Law Dictionary defines 'bona fide' as '[m]ade in good faith; without fraud or deceit,' and '[s]incere; genuine.' (11th ed. 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as reference for evaluating whether transactions or agreements (e.g., sale of business) are genuine or devised to evade legal prohibitions. See Bosley Med. Grp. v. Abramson example where court refused to enforce a non-compete devised to accomplish what law otherwise prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is an 'executive officer' for disclosure/coverage purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'executive officer' (for a registrant) means its president, any vice president in charge of a principal business unit, division or function, any officer who performs a policy making function, or any other person who performs similar policy making functions for the registrant; executive officers of subsidiaries may be deemed executive officers of the registrant if they perform such policy-making functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 17 CFR 240.3b-7 and 17 CFR 240.3b-2 which define 'officer' and 'executive officer' for securities/regulatory purposes. Relevant to assessing who counts as a 'senior executive' under per-company limitations or reporting frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private companies may avoid 'per-company' limitations via restructuring
rubrics_metrics.description: While reporting obligations of public companies may incentivize avoiding generation of many 'senior executives,' privately held companies could potentially avoid per-company limitations through corporate restructuring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes this structural avoidance risk when considering per-company limitations and the differing incentives of public versus private firms (NPRM discussion).
